https://www.mediafax.ro/english/the-russ.text: The Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Romania’s representative in Moscow, Liliana Burda According to available information, Russian authorities did not specify the reason for summoning the Romanian diplomat. The summons comes amid tense relations between Russia and European Union and NATO member states, including Romania. In fact, at the end of July, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MAE) summoned the Russian Federation’s ambassador to Bucharest in response to repeated violations of Romania’s airspace between July 24 and 26, when the Romanian Army shot down three drones that had entered the country’s territory without authorization. At the end of the meeting, a Russian diplomat was officially notified that he had been declared persona non grata and must leave Romania within five days. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced that the Ambassador of the Russian Federation had been summoned to the ministry’s headquarters at the direction of Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu to be informed of Romania’s official protest against the repeated violations of its national airspace. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, between July 24 and 26, the Romanian Army shot down three drones that had entered the country’s territory without authorization. During the meeting, Romanian officials presented the ambassador with fragments from one of the destroyed drones, and the Ministry states that investigations conducted by the Prosecutor’s Office have officially confirmed that they are of Russian origin. The Romanian side lodged a strong protest against what it described as illegal and irresponsible actions and emphasized that the Russian Federation bears sole responsibility for the incidents. The Ministry stated that it is “absolutely unacceptable and intolerable” for Russia to continue violating Romania’s airspace, emphasizing that this airspace is also that of NATO and the European Union. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, these actions contribute to the deterioration of the security situation in the region. The Russian ambassador to Bucharest’s first reaction The Russian ambassador to Bucharest’s first reaction, after being summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding the drones, was not long in coming. Vladimir Lipaev described the protest lodged by the Romanian authorities—after the Romanian Armed Forces shot down three drones that had entered the country’s airspace without authorization—as a “propaganda stunt.” He said that the expulsion of an employee of the Russian Embassy in Bucharest “will not go without an appropriate response” from Moscow. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MAE) confirms that Romania’s chargé d’affaires a.i. in Moscow has been summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation, scheduled for Thursday, August 27, 2026. According to the MFA, Romania assumes that this summons comes in response to the diplomatic measures adopted by Romanian authorities in the context of the wave of drone incidents triggered by the war of aggression waged by the Russian Federation in Ukraine. The summons of the Romanian diplomat comes amid escalating tensions in the region, caused by the war in Ukraine and the drone incidents that have prompted diplomatic reactions from Romania. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not, as of yet, provided further details regarding the discussions scheduled to take place in Moscow. https://www.nbcnews.com/world/russia/rus.text: The Kremlin orchestrated a murder-for-hire plot against a prominent Russian dissident in Washington this summer, according to the Justice Department, which unsealed charges against five people it alleges were part of a “global assassination network” aimed at causing “destruction and mayhem around the world.” The five people are still at large, the Justice Department said in the indictment, which was unsealed late Tuesday, describing the wider operation being run by Russian intelligence as “brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching.” The FBI said it had disrupted the plot, although officials did not detail how. Since at least 2024, the network is alleged to have paid Americans and foreigners to spy on targets, “carry out targeted killings” and “commit acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine,” the Justice Department said. Asked for a response to the allegations by NBC News, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily briefing call with reporters that “until we have heard or seen any reasonable evidence and arguments based on at least something tangible, we do not consider it necessary to comment on this news.” Western governments have accused Russia for decades of carrying out attempted and successful killings abroad. Despite substantial evidence, it has always denied the allegations. The indictment did not name the intended victim in Washington. The Justice Department lists the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, known as “Colonel Yuri,” 63, and his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, both of Russia; Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as “Viking,” both 35 and Cuban nationals; and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, of Venezuela. The indictment describes Durruthy as “an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia,” where, it says, Suarez and Castro also reside. All face a charge of conspiracy to finance terrorism. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro face an additional charge of conspiracy to commit murder for hire. Yuri Khrameev is alleged to be a former Russian intelligence colonel, while his son is an officer in Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. Prosecutors allege the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn, New York, this summer, promising him between $1,000 and $1,500 to photograph and record two locations associated with the Washington target. The man carried out the surveillance but declined an offer from Suarez and Castro of $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target himself, prosecutors said. The alleged recruiters asked whether he knew somebody who would. Suarez also offered substantial sums of money to other people in the U.S. to finish the job, the indictment says. The indictment quotes messages that prosecutors said show the conspirators referred to murder as “construction.” Surveillance instructions included putting the man’s phone into airplane mode and recording while passing the house. Suarez is alleged to have said that he also had people in Mexico who could carry out the killing but that they were delayed. Authorities allege a second plot involving a dissident believed to be living in Lithuania whom the network accused of making derogatory statements about Russia. In that case, a U.S. citizen was promised $200 to photograph the target’s address last year and then was offered around $25,000 to kill him, prosecutors said. When he refused, Yuri Khrameev offered a “simpler job,” prosecutors said — setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electricity substation. The purpose, Khrameev is alleged to have said, was to target “all the countries that are helping Ukraine.” Durruthy, meanwhile, is accused of coordinating logistics for attacks in Prague in June 2024 and Lithuania that September. Lithuanian authorities publicly named Durruthy as wanted in January in a case involving attempts to burn military equipment intended for Ukraine, according to the Lithuanian broadcaster LRT. “These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” said John A. Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security. “Actions like these represent a gross violation of our sovereignty and a threat to our national security,” he said. James C. Barnacle Jr., head of New York’s FBI office, said the agency “disrupted this operation through relentless work and rock-solid partnership.”

https://artdaily.com/news/200505/Jewish-.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact Jewish Museum presents major exhibition of Jewish ritual art and Christian cathedral treasures Spice Container, Germany, c. 1550. Silver: traced, pierced, cast, and parcel-gilt. The Jewish Museum, New York. Photo by Kris Graves. NEW YORK, NY .- The Jewish Museum presents a major exhibition this fall that brings Jewish and Christian sacred art from medieval to early modern Europe into dialogue, illuminating complex, interconnected histories across more than six centuries. Sacred Splendor: Jewish Ritual Art and Christian Treasures from St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague features Christian reliquaries on loan from St. Vitus Cathedral—the most extensive presentation of this treasury ever exhibited outside Europe—together with Jewish treasures never before shown in the United States. Through a robust presentation of over 160 objects, the exhibition examines shared urban and artistic environments, and the distinct ritual and theological frameworks that shaped sacred art across Central Europe. Highlights include rarely seen medieval Jewish-owned objects from hoards buried during periods of persecution that remained hidden for centuries, as well as Jewish ceremonial works from Bohemia and the Germanic regions, among them Torah ornaments, metalwork, and manuscripts. On view from September 18, 2026, through February 7, 2027, the exhibition also features tehillim [Psalms] (2018) by contemporary artist Edmund de Waal, whose work engages interculturally with history, memory, and language. tehillim’s spare composition of ceramic, alabaster, and gold leaf resonates powerfully with surviving fragments from medieval Jewish hoards that are also on view, engaging with the Book of Psalms as “songs and poems of exile.” Concurrently, in the Museum’s new third-floor collection galleries, a series of focused contemporary installations will expand on Sacred Splendor ’s themes. Featuring artists Hannah Altman and Afruz Amighi, these presentations dialogue with the themes and materiality of the treasures on display from St. Vitus Cathedral and other sources across Europe and the United States. “Sacred Splendor offers a monumental illustration of cultural exchange that demonstrates the shared aesthetics which defined sacred art for Christian and Jewish communities alike from Late Antiquity through the 19th Century,” said James S. Snyder, Helen Goldsmith Menschel Director. “We are thrilled to present stunningly crafted reliquaries from St. Vitus Cathedral together with rare Jewish treasures from the same time notably bringing the Lingenfeld, Weissenfels, and Środa Śląska hoards together for the first time in the U.S. While serving as iconic examples of Christian and Jewish ritual art, these objects also tell stories of the Jewish and Christian experiences of migration, assimilation, and resilience throughout time and across the global diaspora.” The exhibition’s narrative is anchored in the city of Prague, a religious and political capital at the crossroads of Central European trade routes that emerged as a key medieval center for the production of sacred art. King of Bohemia Charles IV refashioned the city’s St. Vitus Cathedral into a Gothic marvel and endowed it with important relics, commissioning elaborate reliquaries to house them. Prague’s Jewish community, well-established during this period after settling in the city centuries earlier, lived in close proximity to its Christian neighbors, developing their ritual traditions alongside one another. “Sacred art from medieval and early modern Central Europe emerged from a shared urban world—shaped by the same trade routes, the same cities, often the same artistic workshops,” said Abigail Rapoport, Jack, Joseph and Morton Mandel Curator of Judaica. "Sacred Splendor brings that world into focus through singular objects, illuminating the visual culture that gave rise to these objects—and the forms of ritual art that continue to shape religious life today." Organized chronologically and thematically, the exhibition sheds light on the ways in which a shared built environment —including Gothic architecture and design—influenced stylistic developments across faiths, producing visual resonances between sacred objects. Since Jews were barred from joining professional guilds, Christian artisans often worked across Jewish and Christian communities. The same Christian masons built Prague’s Altneuschul Synagogue and the nearby Convent of St. Agnes, from which architectural fragments will be on view. Similarly, a Christian Prayer Book and an illustrated Hebrew Bible from the workshop of the late fifteenth-century Bohemian illuminator Valentine Noh will be shown together for the first time. Against the backdrop of this shared artistic environment, ties between Christians and Jews in Central Europe often frayed. When plague swept across Europe in the late 1340s, fear and uncertainty overwhelmed already-fragile social relations. Jews were falsely accused of poisoning water wells and causing the Black Death, which led to widespread attacks, expulsions, and the destruction of long-established Jewish communities across Central Europe. Some affluent Jewish families, facing escalating threat, hid their silver, coins, and jewelry underground, including several groups of objects showcased in the exhibition. These hoards stand in stark juxtaposition to the Christian reliquaries preserved by the church with reverence over hundreds of years. Sacred Splendor concludes in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries when Jewish ritual life flourished, book production blossomed, and vibrant cultural exchange thrived. This period was marked by the construction of three new synagogues in Prague, the establishment of communal organizations—including the first modern burial society—and a robust Hebrew printing culture. “At the heart of this exhibition is how the spiritual manifests differently in the traditions of Judaism and Christianity,” said Claudia Nahson, Morris & Eva Feld Senior Curator. “While Christian reliquaries are repositories of material fragments associated with sacred figures, making the sacred visible, the spirit of Jewish faith, embodied by its objects of ceremonial practice, is primarily rooted in the oral and textual transmission of tradition and the centrality of the Torah.” Publication The exhibition is accompanied by a richly illustrated catalogue authored by the exhibition co-curators, with a contribution by leading medieval art historian Jiří Fajt. The publication presents new scholarship and numerous reproductions of rarely seen works. A special section features conversations between Leon Levy Associate Curator Shira Backer and the contemporary artists whose work is included in the exhibition and the companion installation in the Museum’s collection galleries. https://www.politico.eu/article/pedro-sa.text: SEVILLE, Spain — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez officially launched his long-shot reelection bid in Seville on Thursday, appealing to Socialist loyalists in Andalusia, the southern region that for decades served as his party’s political heartland. But even here, the center-left is now is on the ropes — in a stark sign of how improbable a Sánchez win now looks on Nov. 29. Surrounded by Socialist supporters waving red party banners and Andalusian flags and shouting “ ¡Guapo! ” — “Handsome!” — the undaunted prime minister took the stage in Seville, dancing to the upbeat strains of a romantic pop song, chosen to underscore his progressive message of love in the face of the politics of hate. Advertisement Advertisement “We’re here to vote, we’re here to win, we’re here to govern,” Sánchez told the adoring crowd, which had been shown videos of the prime minister reciting poems by Federico García Lorca, the celebrated Andalusian poet and playwright murdered by Francoist forces in 1936. Sánchez’s decision to launch his campaign in Seville is laden with historic symbolism. For 36 years, the Socialists dominated Andalusian politics, controlling the regional government and many of the region’s biggest cities. That hold on power ended in 2018, after years of declining support and a string of corruption scandals paved the way for the center-right People’s Party to take control. Since becoming regional president in 2019, Juanma Moreno has established himself as a steady, pragmatic leader, winning a landslide victory in 2022 and securing the most votes in snap elections earlier this year. His success in Andalusia has also elevated his profile nationally, making him one of the leading figures of the PP’s moderate wing. Despite the PP’s consolidation of power in Andalusia, the Socialists are not ready to relinquish their claim on the region. Francisco Toscano, a Socialist candidate for congress in Seville, told POLITICO the party still considered Andalusia to be its bastion. “This is an eminently progressive region, and one whose voters believe in progressive government,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Electorally, he added, Andalusia is crucial to the Socialists’ grander ambitions. “This is the most populous autonomous community in Spain, so its weight at the national level is very important,” he continued, noting that the region elects the largest number of lawmakers to the parliament in Madrid, making up 60 of the 350 seats. But while Sánchez’s campaign launch struck an optimistic note about the prospect of an Andalusian comeback, the latest polling suggests the Socialists could suffer disastrous results across the region. According to the latest GAD3 poll , the center-right People’s Party is ahead of the Socialists in most Andalusian provinces — including Seville, where Sánchez’s party has never previously lost in a general election. A rout in Andalusia would be more than a regional setback for Sánchez. It would further narrow his slim path to reelection , making a fresh national mandate look all the more out of reach. Reversal of fortune The Socialists’ decline in Andalusia is, in many ways, a consequence of their own success. When the party first came to power in the region in 1982, Andalusia was one of Spain’s poorest areas. But under leaders such as Manuel Chaves — who ruled the region for 19 years — it underwent a profound transformation. Advertisement Advertisement Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, Socialist regional governments used EU structural funds to spur economic development, funding infrastructure projects such as the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway. Between 1982 and 1996, Socialist Prime Minister Felipe González — a proud native son on Seville — championed the region from Madrid, helping secure major investments and backing landmark events such as the Expo ’92 World’s Fair , which brought a fresh wave of investment to Andalusia. But as regional living standards improved, voters’ expectations rose too — and the party increasingly struggled to meet them. “There was a paradox of satisfaction,” said Ángel Cazorla, a political scientist at the University of Granada. “Although Andalusians felt the Socialists had overseen decades of progress, and personally felt their lives had improved, the great recession exposed how much remained unfinished or unresolved.” By 2018, frustration over persistent problems such as unemployment and strained public services, and corruption cases involving high-ranking regional grandees, ultimately led to the Socialists’ ouster. Cazorla said the two deadly train accidents that rocked Spain this year, both of which occurred on the iconic Madrid-Seville rail line, were emblematic of the party’s decline. Advertisement Advertisement “In addition to the human toll, we can list Curro as a victim of these tragedies,” he said, referring to the colorful cartoon bird that served as the mascot of the 1992 Seville World’s Fair and which many Andalusians associate with the prosperity of the Socialist era. “The deadly accidents are in a lot of ways representative of a social-democratic project that gradually ran out of steam, and that successive governments have failed to look after what had been achieved not only with infrastructure, but public goods and overall quality of life,” he added. The generational gap Socialist candidate Toscano is not blind to the reasons the Socialists have lost ground. After decades in power, he acknowledged, the party had faced growing pressure from the right, corruption scandals and a failure to adapt its message to changing living standards. “We had shortcomings in our management in recent years,” he said, while arguing the Socialists had nonetheless remained electorally competitive in parts of the region. Cazorla argued the party’s difficulties go beyond its record in government: It also faces a generational problem. Younger electors who grew up in an already-transformed Andalusia feel little identification with the Socialists or with a regional leadership associated with the discredited administrations of the past. “A young left-wing voter is paying attention to a different message — one the old guard is incapable of projecting,” he said, adding Adelante Andalucía, a regionalist party that advocates in favor of greater self-government and left-wing policies, is more likely to seduce local electors. Toscano, however, remained hopeful that Andalusian voters would turn out for the Socialists in an election he frames as a choice between Sánchez’s progressive agenda and the global conservative wave. “We’ve seen public services deteriorate under Giorgia Meloni in Italy, and Javier Milei wielding his ‘chainsaw’ to dismantle Argentina’s welfare state,” he said. “In this election, Spaniards must choose whether to remain a country that continues to make social progress or follow the path of regression we are seeing elsewhere.” Advertisement Advertisement
